title: Should You File for Divorce Before the End of the Year in Colorado?

tags.name: Managed URL by Permalink Manager Lite

content.rendered:
Timing your divorce filing probably isn’t the first thing on your mind when everything in your life already feels upside-down. But here’s the truth most people don’t realize: when you file can have real-world consequences—financial, legal, and emotional.

For many Coloradans, the weeks leading up to December 31 end up being a surprisingly strategic time to file. Not because it’s fun (it isn’t), but because the calendar impacts everything from tax consequences to court delay to who ends up responsible for holiday spending.

Colorado Revised Statutes § 14-10-113 governs how property and debts are divided—and the timing of your filing can affect how certain financial pieces get classified. So if you’re on the fence, it’s worth understanding what actually changes when the year flips.

Here are five reasons people in Colorado often choose to file before the new year.

1.Your Taxes for Next Year Become Way More Predictable

Like it or not, the IRS plays by one simple rule: your marital status on December 31 controls your filing status for that entire tax year.

If you file before year-end, you may:

  • avoid an argument about whether you’re filing jointly or separately,
  • prevent disputes over deductions or child-related credits, and
  • eliminate the possibility of being dragged into an unwanted “married filing jointly” return.

When finances are already tense, cleaning up next year’s tax picture can be a huge relief.

2.Colorado Courts Get Slammed in January — You Can Beat the Rush

Every year, family courts in Colorado see an avalanche of new filings the first week of January. Everyone who “held it together for the holidays” hits the courthouse at the same time.

That backlog trickles down to:

  • slower hearing dates,
  • delayed mediation timelines,
  • and longer waits for temporary orders (which you may need for parenting or financial stability).

If you file before December 31, you’re essentially stepping into line before the rush hits—and that can move your case along faster when time matters.

3.You Protect Yourself From the Financial Chaos of the Holidays

Holiday spending—gifts, trips, dinners, Amazon “oops” purchases—adds up fast. And under CRS § 14-10-113, debt incurred during the marriage is typically classified as marital.

If your spouse tends to overspend, or the two of you disagree about holiday budgets, filing before year-end draws a bright legal line between:

  • marital debt that existed before the filing, and
  • new debt your spouse racks up afterward.

This isn’t about being petty. It’s about not getting stuck footing the bill for a holiday you didn’t agree to.

4.You Start the New Year With Clarity Instead of Carrying the Weight

Here’s something clients say again and again:
“The moment I filed, I could finally breathe.”

You’re not rushing the decision—you’re giving it structure. Filing before year-end lets you step into January with:

  • a plan,
  • a timeline,
  • temporary protections if needed,
  • and a clear sense of direction instead of dread.

It’s not dramatic. It’s stabilizing.

5.Parents Get a Head Start on Parenting Plans

If you have kids, filing earlier gives you more time to establish temporary parenting orders before spring schedules get complicated.

Colorado courts prioritize the best interests of the child, and early temporary orders can help:

  • reduce co-parent conflict,
  • provide stability during the school year,
  • manage extracurriculars and childcare clearly,
  • and give kids predictability during a chaotic time.

Waiting until January can push everything months down the road, which only increases tension.

Should You File Before December 31?

Not everyone needs to. But for many Colorado residents, filing before year-end offers advantages in taxes, timing, finances, and parenting stability. What matters is your situation and your goals—not the calendar alone.
